# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

Static Single Assignment form requires each variable to have exactly one static definition, with control-flow merges resolved by **phi-functions**. The classical approach, due to **Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck**, computes the **dominator tree** (via Lengauer-Tarjan or the simpler iterative dataflow algorithm), then computes **dominance frontiers**: DF(n) is the set of nodes m such that n dominates a predecessor of m but does not strictly dominate m itself. Phi-functions for a variable v are placed at the iterated dominance frontier of v's definition sites (DF⁺, the closure of DF under union over the def set), because that is precisely where two distinct definitions of v can reach along different paths. After placement, **variable renaming** proceeds via a preorder DFS of the dominator tree, maintaining a per-variable rename stack: each definition pushes a new SSA name, each use reads the stack top, and stack entries are popped when the DFS backtracks out of a block's dominance subtree.

A more implementation-friendly alternative is **Braun et al.'s "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form"**, which builds SSA directly during a single pass over the CFG without precomputing dominance frontiers. Variable lookups recurse upward through predecessors; if a block has multiple predecessors and is not yet **sealed** (i.e., not all predecessors are known, as in irreducible or not-yet-generated loop back-edges), an **incomplete phi-function** is inserted as a placeholder. Once a block is sealed, pending phi operands are resolved. Trivial phi-functions — those whose operands are all identical or self-referential — are removed via a **trivial-phi-removal/simplification** step that recursively coalesces phi chains, which also naturally produces **minimal SSA** without a separate minimality pass.

A third concern is **pruned vs. semi-pruned SSA**: naive placement at every iterated dominance frontier node produces dead phi-functions for variables not live across that merge. Semi-pruned SSA avoids inserting phis for variables never live out of basic blocks (computed via a cheap one-pass liveness approximation), while fully pruned SSA uses true liveness analysis to place phis only where the variable is actually live, trading analysis cost for code size. **SSA destruction** (out-of-SSA translation) is the dual problem: phi-functions must be eliminated before register allocation on conventional architectures, which requires inserting copies at predecessor blocks. Naive copy insertion can introduce the **lost-copy problem** (a value overwritten before use due to parallel-copy semantics not being respected) and the **swap problem** (two variables needing simultaneous exchange). These are resolved by treating phi-elimination as a parallel-copy sequentialization problem, or by maintaining **conventional SSA** (interference-free congruence classes between phi-related variables) throughout optimization so destruction becomes trivial copy insertion, often combined with **live-range splitting** to break interference before coalescing.

## 2. Alias Analysis

Alias analysis determines whether two pointer expressions may, must, or cannot reference the same memory location, classifying results as **must-alias**, **may-alias**, or **no-alias**. **Andersen's analysis** is inclusion-based: it generates subset constraints of the form pts(a) ⊇ pts(b) for assignments, builds a constraint graph where points-to sets propagate along edges, and iterates propagation (often with **cycle elimination** via SCC collapsing of cells known to have identical points-to sets) to a fixed point. It is flow-insensitive and context-insensitive by default, with worst-case O(n³) complexity because edges can be added dynamically as points-to sets grow, each triggering further propagation.

**Steensgaard's analysis** instead unifies the points-to sets of a and b whenever an assignment a = b occurs, using a **union-find** data structure over abstract storage locations. This collapses variables into equivalence classes eagerly, losing precision (two variables that merely sometimes alias become permanently aliased) but achieving near-linear time, making it attractive for quick, whole-program passes where precision is secondary to scalability.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA)**, used extensively in LLVM and C/C++ frontends, exploits the language's **strict aliasing rule**: an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of its **effective type** (or compatible type, or char*). The compiler attaches TBAA metadata describing each memory access's static type and, in LLVM's **struct-path-sensitive TBAA**, the full access path (struct type plus field offset) rather than just the base type, enabling disambiguation between accesses to different fields of the same struct type. TBAA is unsound under type-punning that violates strict aliasing, which is why -fno-strict-aliasing disables it.

Precision dimensions orthogonal to the three algorithms above include **flow-sensitivity** (whether points-to sets vary per program point or are computed once globally), **context-sensitivity** (distinguishing call sites via **k-CFA** or the **call-string approach**, which tags abstract locations with bounded call-site history), and **field-sensitivity** (modeling individual struct fields rather than treating aggregates monolithically). Results feed directly into **load/store forwarding** (replacing a load with a prior store's value when no-alias or must-alias is proven between them), **dead store elimination** (removing a store proven never read before being overwritten, which requires no intervening may-alias access), and **LICM** (hoisting a loop-invariant load out of a loop requires proving no store inside the loop may-aliases it).

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin-Briggs graph-coloring allocation** builds an **interference graph** where nodes are live ranges (virtual registers) and edges connect ranges live simultaneously. Allocation proceeds via **simplify-spill-select**: repeatedly remove nodes of degree less than k (the number of physical registers) and push them on a stack (simplify); if no such node exists, optimistically pick a **spill candidate** by a cost heuristic (typically uses/defs weighted by loop depth divided by degree) and push it anyway, deferring the spill decision (**optimistic coloring**, Briggs's refinement of Chaitin's original pessimistic spill-on-push approach); then pop the stack and assign colors (select), only materializing an actual spill if no color remains available. **Coalescing** merges move-related nodes to eliminate copy instructions; **Briggs conservative coalescing** merges two nodes only if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k, while **Chaitin aggressive/biased coalescing** merges more eagerly but risks uncolorable graphs, requiring more conservative fallback.

**Linear scan register allocation** (Poletto and Sarkar) avoids building an explicit interference graph. It computes **live intervals** (a contiguous or union-of-ranges approximation of liveness) for each virtual register, sorts intervals by start point, and sweeps through them maintaining an **active list** of currently live intervals assigned to physical registers. When a new interval starts and no register is free, the allocator spills the active interval with the **furthest next use** (or furthest endpoint in the simplest formulation), which is provably optimal for minimizing spills in the single-register-class, no-coalescing case (Belady's farthest-in-future argument). Extensions like **second-chance/extended linear scan** allow previously spilled values to be reloaded into registers for later subranges rather than staying memory-resident for the whole interval, narrowing the gap with graph-coloring quality while retaining near-linear-time complexity, which is why it dominates JIT compilers (JVM C1, early V8) under compile-time pressure.

**SSA-based register allocation** exploits the fact that the interference graph of values in strict SSA form is **chordal** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord), because liveness in SSA corresponds to dominance-tree structure. Chordal graphs are colorable in polynomial time via a **perfect elimination ordering**, making greedy coloring exact (no NP-hardness obstruction) without the simplify-spill heuristic's approximation. LLVM's **greedy register allocator** builds on this lineage: it processes live ranges ordered by spill weight and size, attempts direct assignment, and on failure performs **live-range splitting** (dividing an interval at a program point to reduce interference, e.g., around a loop) or **eviction** (bumping a lower-priority already-assigned range) before resorting to spill code insertion. Supporting mechanisms across all approaches include **rematerialization** (recomputing a cheap value instead of reloading it from a spill slot) and careful **spill code placement** at points minimizing dynamic execution frequency (e.g., outside loops), both of which interact with register-pressure estimates partitioned by register class (GPR, FPR, vector).

## 4. Inlining

Cost-benefit inlining, as implemented in GCC and LLVM, computes an **inline cost model**: a static estimate of the callee's size (instruction count weighted by target-specific cost) compared against a threshold, adjusted by **bonus heuristics** — e.g., a call site where an argument is a compile-time constant earns a bonus because it is likely to enable downstream **constant propagation** and dead-branch elimination inside the callee, and a call through a pointer that can be resolved to a direct call earns a devirtualization bonus. The overall transformation is bounded by a **growth budget** controlling total caller size increase, and **recursive inlining limits** (inlining depth caps or recursion-cycle detection in the call graph) prevent unbounded expansion.

**Profile-guided inlining** uses PGO edge and block execution counts to prioritize call sites by actual hotness rather than static heuristics alone: hot call sites receive a relaxed size threshold (since the runtime benefit of eliminating call overhead and exposing further optimization at a hot site outweighs code growth), while cold call sites are deprioritized or left uninlined to control code size (and, relatedly, instruction-cache pressure). **Speculative inlining with guards**, common in JIT compilers, inlines a monomorphic or dominant-type call site behind a runtime type check (**guard**); if the guard fails, control falls back to an uninlined/interpreted path, and repeated failure triggers **deoptimization**.

**Devirtualization** mechanisms determine when a virtual/polymorphic call can become inlinable. **Class hierarchy analysis (CHA)** statically proves a virtual call has only one possible target by analyzing the finalized class hierarchy (no further overriding subclasses can be loaded, which is why CHA is more powerful in closed-world/whole-program settings and must be invalidated or guarded in dynamically-loading systems like the JVM). **Speculative devirtualization** inserts a guard comparing the receiver's runtime type (or vtable pointer) against the hypothesized type and inlines the direct call on the fast path, falling back to a virtual call otherwise. **Polymorphic inline caches (PICs)**, used in V8 and HotSpot, extend this by caching multiple (type, target) pairs observed at a call site, allowing inlining of a small switch over the few observed receiver types instead of a full virtual dispatch, directly informed by runtime type feedback collected during earlier interpreted/baseline execution.

Pass ordering matters: **early inlining** (pre-optimization, exposing more context for subsequent scalar optimizations like SROA and constant folding) is distinguished from **late inlining** (post-optimization, for cases where early decisions would have been premature, e.g., after loop-invariant costs are known). Call-graph traversal order is typically **bottom-up** (leaves inlined into callers first, so cost estimates reflect already-inlined callees) with **SCC-based** handling for recursive cycles in the call graph (treating a strongly-connected component as a unit and bounding inlining within it to avoid infinite expansion).

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph escape analysis**, the model used in HotSpot (following Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, and Midkiff), builds a graph of **object nodes** (allocation sites), **phantom nodes** (representing unknown objects from outside the analyzed scope, e.g., objects passed in as parameters), **field edges** (object-to-object edges representing field assignments), and **deferred edges** (representing that a variable's pointed-to object at this point equals another variable's, resolved like a copy). Each object node is labeled with an **escape state**: **NoEscape** (the object is provably confined to the current method/thread and never stored into an escaping location or passed to an unanalyzable call), **ArgEscape** (the object escapes via being passed as an argument but does not escape the thread globally), or **GlobalEscape** (the object may be reachable from outside the method or thread, e.g., stored into a static field or returned).

These escape states directly license two downstream transformations. **Scalar replacement of aggregates (SRoA)**, when applied to a NoEscape allocation, replaces the object's individual fields with independent scalar SSA values (or decomposed stack slots), eliminating the heap allocation entirely and letting each field participate in ordinary scalar optimization (constant propagation, dead code elimination) rather than being opaque heap memory. **Stack allocation** is the coarser-grained version: a NoEscape object that cannot be fully scalarized (e.g., due to escaping references within a complex control flow) can still be allocated on the stack frame instead of the heap, avoiding garbage collection pressure. A related consequence is **synchronization elimination/lock elision**: if a monitor object is proven NoEscape (thread-local), the JIT can remove its associated monitorenter/monitorexit instructions outright, since no other thread can ever observe or contend for that lock — distinct from (and stronger than) biased locking, which optimizes the common uncontended case without removing synchronization.

Escape analysis can be **flow-sensitive** (tracking escape state changes along control-flow paths precisely) or **flow-insensitive** (computing one summary per allocation site, cheaper but less precise), and **intraprocedural** vs. **interprocedural/whole-program** (the latter propagating escape information across method boundaries via summaries, necessary to avoid conservatively marking every object passed to a callee as escaping). Escape analysis has a tight feedback loop with **inlining**: inlining a callee exposes its body directly into the caller's analysis scope, which frequently turns an ArgEscape classification (object passed to an opaque call) into NoEscape (the "call" is now visible inlined code that provably doesn't leak the reference), which is why escape analysis is typically scheduled after an inlining pass in JIT pipelines.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**Classic loop vectorization** legality rests on **dependence analysis**: for each pair of array accesses across loop iterations, a **distance vector** or **direction vector** characterizes the dependence (e.g., distance +1 means iteration i depends on i-1). Exact dependence testing uses the **GCD test** (checking integer solvability of the linear Diophantine subscript equation) as a cheap necessary condition, refined by the **Banerjee test** or the more general **Omega test** (integer linear programming over the iteration space) for precise feasibility when GCD is inconclusive. If no dependence with a backward (lexicographically negative) direction exists across the vectorized dimension, the loop can be vectorized. The transformation itself is **strip-mining**: rewriting the loop to iterate in chunks of the target vector width, with the inner chunk executed as a single vector instruction.

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization**, from Larsen and Amarasinghe, is a complementary technique operating on straight-line code rather than loop trip counts: it identifies **isomorphic statements** (same opcode, compatible operand structure) that are mutually independent, groups them into a **pack**, and recursively extends packs through their operands and users, building a pack graph that is then lowered to vector instructions with explicit pack/unpack (shuffle) glue code at the pack graph's boundaries. Unlike loop vectorization, SLP requires no loop structure at all — it vectorizes sequences like four scalar struct-field additions appearing adjacently in a basic block.

The **LLVM Loop Vectorizer** operationalizes classic loop vectorization with several concrete mechanisms: a **cost model** evaluates candidate **vectorization factors (VF)** (e.g., 2, 4, 8 lanes) by estimating instruction cost per VF against scalar cost, selecting the VF (and a separate **interleaving/unrolling factor** to hide latency and improve register-level parallelism) that minimizes estimated cost per element. **Reduction recognition** identifies accumulation patterns (sum, min/max) and transforms them into vector-wide partial reductions with a final horizontal reduction step. **Induction variable widening** transforms a scalar induction variable into a vector of consecutive values incremented by VF each iteration. **Masked/predicated vectorization** handles divergent control flow (if-conversion inside the loop body) by converting conditional statements into predicated vector operations using mask registers, avoiding the need to scalarize branchy loops. For the **remainder/tail** iterations that don't fill a full vector, the vectorizer chooses between a **scalar epilogue loop** (simple, always correct) or a **masked tail** using vector predication to handle the remainder within the vector loop itself (avoiding a separate scalar loop, valuable on architectures with efficient predication like AVX-512 or SVE).

Supporting analyses include **alignment analysis** (determining whether accesses are naturally aligned to enable aligned loads/stores rather than slower unaligned ones), cost-model tradeoffs between wider SIMD and increased **register pressure** (a VF too large can force spills, negating vectorization's benefit), and **gather/scatter** instructions for non-unit-stride memory accesses that cannot be expressed as contiguous vector loads/stores.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling** operates over a **data dependence graph (DDG)** built per basic block (or larger scheduling region), with edges for **true (read-after-write)**, **anti (write-after-read)**, and **output (write-after-write)** dependences, each annotated with latency. A **priority function** — commonly the **critical-path length** (longest latency-weighted path from a node to a DAG sink) — ranks ready instructions (those whose predecessors are already scheduled) at each cycle; the scheduler picks the highest-priority ready instruction subject to resource constraints (functional unit availability). Scheduling can proceed **top-down** (ASAP-oriented, scheduling from the DAG's roots forward) or **bottom-up** (ALAP-oriented, scheduling from sinks backward), with bottom-up often preferred because it naturally favors delaying instructions whose results aren't needed yet, reducing register pressure.

**Software pipelining via iterative modulo scheduling** targets loops directly, overlapping iterations to exploit ILP across iteration boundaries. It first computes the **minimum initiation interval (MII)** as the maximum of the **resource-constrained MII** (total resource demand per iteration divided by resource count) and the **recurrence-constrained MII** (longest latency cycle in the dependence graph, which bounds how fast iterations can start due to intra-loop recurrences like accumulations). The scheduler then iteratively attempts to schedule instructions into a **modulo reservation table** (a cyclic resource-usage table of size equal to the candidate initiation interval), incrementing the interval and retrying on resource conflicts, until a legal schedule is found. The resulting steady-state **kernel** is wrapped with **prologue** code (filling the pipeline for the first overlapped iterations) and **epilogue** code (draining it for the last), which is the direct instruction-level analog of hardware pipeline fill/drain.

**Trace scheduling** (and its simpler relative, **superblock scheduling**) extends ILP exploitation across basic block boundaries by first selecting a **trace** — a likely linear execution path through multiple basic blocks — using profile data to pick the most frequently taken branch direction at each merge. Instructions are then scheduled as if the trace were a single block, including **speculative code motion above branches** (hoisting an instruction from below a branch to above it, executing it even on paths where it wasn't originally needed, as long as it's safe/undoable). When control flow actually diverges from the selected trace (an off-trace jump), **compensation code** must be inserted at the trace's side exits to preserve correctness, replicating any effects that speculative motion assumed would happen.

Scheduling variants include **top-down vs. bottom-up** direction choice (discussed above) and, for **VLIW** targets, **bundle packing**: the scheduler must simultaneously respect hazard constraints and pack independent instructions into fixed-width issue bundles, often guided by the same list-scheduling priority machinery with an added bundling/packing step. A persistent complication is the **phase-ordering problem between scheduling and register allocation**: scheduling before allocation (**pre-pass scheduling**) can increase register pressure by extending live ranges to fill gaps, causing allocator-inserted spills to later disrupt the schedule, while scheduling after allocation (**post-pass scheduling**) must respect allocation decisions already baked in, including false anti-dependences introduced by register reuse that pre-pass scheduling never had to deal with; most production pipelines run both a pre-pass and a post-pass scheduler to balance the tradeoff.

## 8. Loop Optimizations (general)

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)** identifies computations whose operands are all defined outside the loop (or are themselves loop-invariant, computed transitively) using the SSA dominance property — a loop-invariant instruction's hoisted position in the **loop preheader** must dominate all uses, which SSA's single-definition property makes straightforward to verify. Hoisting a load requires alias analysis to prove no intervening store in the loop body may-alias it; when hoisting is unsafe for all paths but safe along some, **speculative hoisting with sinking** (or **loop-invariant code sinking** for the dual case of partially dead computations) relocates code to the point where it's unconditionally safe and profitable.

**Loop unrolling** replicates the loop body multiple times to amortize loop-control overhead and expose more ILP; **full unrolling** (eliminating the loop entirely) is applied when trip count is a known small compile-time constant, while **partial unrolling** applies an unroll factor chosen heuristically against code-size growth and estimated trip count. **Unroll-and-jam** extends this to nested loops: the outer loop is unrolled and the resulting copies of the inner loop are then **jammed (fused)** together, improving data reuse across what were formerly separate outer iterations, at the cost of requiring legality checks that the jammed accesses don't violate dependences introduced by the fusion.

**Loop tiling/blocking** partitions iteration space into smaller blocks sized to fit a cache level, trading increased loop nest depth for improved spatial/temporal locality — essential for optimizing dense linear algebra kernels. **Loop interchange** swaps the nesting order of two loops to change the stride pattern of the innermost loop (favoring unit-stride innermost access for locality); its legality is determined by the **dependence direction matrix**: interchange is legal only if the resulting matrix, after swapping the corresponding rows/columns, contains no illegal direction vector pattern (specifically, no dependence whose direction would become "backward" in the new innermost position in a way that violates the original program order).

Additional mechanisms: **induction variable simplification and strength reduction** replace expensive derived computations (e.g., array address calculations involving multiplication by the loop index) with cheaper **derived induction variables** updated by addition each iteration, eliminating multiplications from the loop body. **Loop fusion** merges adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces to improve locality and reduce loop overhead, legal only when dependence analysis shows no fused dependence would reverse direction; its inverse, **loop fission/distribution**, splits a loop into multiple loops when doing so enables other optimizations (e.g., vectorizing one part that was blocked by a dependence in another part). **Loop-closed SSA form (LCSSA)** inserts trivial phi-nodes at loop exit blocks for every value defined inside the loop and used outside it, ensuring all such values have a single well-defined merge point immediately at loop exit, which considerably simplifies subsequent loop transformations (they only need to reason about uses within a clean exit boundary rather than arbitrary uses scattered after the loop). Finally, the **polyhedral model** (used by tools like Pluto and Polly/LLVM) unifies many of the above transformations by representing a loop nest's iteration space as an integer polytope with affine constraints and representing dependences and transformations (interchange, tiling, fusion, skewing) as affine maps over that polytope, enabling a search over a large space of legal affine schedules to optimize for locality and parallelism simultaneously rather than applying transformations as disconnected heuristic passes.

---

# SSA Construction: Dominance Frontiers, Local Construction, and Destruction

## 1. The Cytron–Ferrante–Rosen–Wegman–Zadeck (CFRWZ) Algorithm

The classic algorithm proceeds in three phases built on the dominator tree.

**Dominator tree construction.** A node *d* dominates node *n* (written *d* dom *n*) if every path from the entry to *n* passes through *d*. The immediate dominator idom(*n*) is the unique closest strict dominator, and the dominator tree is the tree formed by idom edges. The standard efficient construction is the Lengauer–Tarjan algorithm, running in O(E log V) (or near-linear with sophisticated union-find), computing idom for all nodes via DFS numbering, semidominators, and a modified union-find with path compression. A simpler iterative data-flow formulation (Cooper, Harvey, Kennedy) computes idom to a fixpoint using reverse postorder and is often preferred for its simplicity at near-equivalent practical performance.

**Dominance frontiers.** Formally, DF(*n*) = { *m* | *n* dominates a predecessor of *m*, but *n* does not strictly dominate *m* }. Intuitively, DF(*n*) is the set of CFG nodes where *n*'s domination "stops" — the first points past *n* where control-flow paths merge that did not all pass through *n*'s strict domination. Cytron et al. compute DF(*n*) for all *n* using the dominator tree via two local relations:

- *DFlocal*(*n*): successors *m* of *n* in the CFG such that *n* does not strictly dominate *m* (this captures join points immediately adjacent to *n*).
- *DFup*(*c*) for a child *c* of *n* in the dominator tree: nodes *w* in DF(*c*) that *n* does not strictly dominate.

DF(*n*) = DFlocal(*n*) ∪ ⋃_{c ∈ children(n)} DFup(c). This is computed bottom-up over the dominator tree in a single post-order traversal, giving overall near-linear complexity in practice, though worst-case DF sets can be quadratic in program size.

**Iterated dominance frontier (IDF) and phi-placement.** For each variable *v* with a set of definition sites Defs(*v*), the minimal set of basic blocks requiring phi-functions is the iterated dominance frontier IDF(Defs(v)) — the limit of the sequence DF(S), DF(S ∪ DF(S)), … until fixpoint. Cytron et al. compute this efficiently using a worklist algorithm annotated with per-node "has-already" and "work" flags keyed by variable, avoiding redundant insertion, giving the phi-placement phase amortized near-linear time per variable (and overall O(V·E) worst case bound, much better in practice).

**Variable renaming.** A single depth-first traversal of the dominator tree renames variables into SSA form. Each original variable *v* has a rename stack; on entering a block, each phi-function gets a fresh SSA name pushed; each use is rewritten to the current top-of-stack name; each definition generates a fresh name pushed onto the stack; before recursing into dominator-tree children, phi-function operands in CFG successors are filled using the current stack tops; upon leaving a block, all pushes made within it are popped. This guarantees the dominance property of SSA (every use is dominated by its unique definition) and runs in O(size of program).

## 2. Braun et al.'s Simple and Efficient SSA Construction

This algorithm avoids explicit dominance computation entirely, building SSA directly during a single forward pass over the CFG (often during initial IR construction), using **local value numbering** per block plus **recursive lookup across predecessors** for cross-block values.

Each block maintains a mapping from variable name to current SSA value (local value numbering table). `writeVariable(var, block, value)` records a definition; `readVariable(var, block)` looks up the local table, and if absent, triggers `readVariableRecursive`:

- If the block is not yet **sealed** (not all predecessors are known, as with a loop header before the loop body is processed), an **incomplete phi-function** (empty operand list) is created and recorded as the current value, deferring operand population.
- If the block has exactly one predecessor, the value is obtained by recursing into that predecessor (no phi needed).
- Otherwise a new phi-function is created, tentatively bound (to break recursive cycles, e.g., in loops), and then its operands are filled in by recursively reading the variable from each predecessor.

**Sealing** a block (once all its predecessors are known/processed) triggers `addPhiOperands` for any pending incomplete phis in it, drawing operand values from each predecessor via `readVariable`.

**Trivial phi-function removal** is applied eagerly: a phi whose operands are all identical (ignoring self-references) is redundant and replaced by that common operand everywhere it is used; this can cascade, requiring revisiting users of the removed phi, and is implemented efficiently by tracking phi users. This produces **minimal SSA** (no redundant phis) without ever computing dominance frontiers explicitly, at the cost of needing a cycle-breaking tentative-phi trick and careful bookkeeping of sealed/unsealed blocks, typically arising naturally from processing blocks in CFG build order with loop headers sealed only after their bodies are linked in.

## 3. SSA Destruction and Related Concepts

**Out-of-SSA translation** replaces phi-functions with ordinary copy instructions so the IR can be lowered to a non-SSA target (e.g., machine code with real registers). The naive approach inserts copies for each phi operand at the end of the corresponding predecessor block (or along the corresponding CFG edge) and a copy into the phi's destination. Two hazards arise:

- **Lost-copy problem**: if a predecessor block has multiple successors, inserting a copy at the end of that block can incorrectly affect the other successor's path; this requires edge splitting (inserting a new block on the critical edge) rather than appending to the predecessor directly.
- **Swap problem**: when phi-functions in a block cyclically permute values from the predecessor (e.g., parallel copies x←y, y←x), naive sequential copy insertion corrupts values; this requires treating phi-resolution as a **parallel copy** (simultaneous assignment) problem, sequentialized correctly via a temporary or copy-sequencing algorithm (Boissinot et al.; sequentializing parallel copies on a DAG of dependencies, using a temp to break cycles).

**Register coalescing** then merges SSA names connected by copies when they do not interfere (do not have overlapping live ranges while holding different values), reducing copy overhead; this is typically done via interference-graph-based coalescing (Chaitin-style, or the more precise SSA-based coalescing that exploits the chordality of SSA interference graphs for exact, non-conservative coalescing). **Live-range splitting** inserts additional copies/renames to break interferences that would otherwise block coalescing or cause spills, trading copy instructions for reduced register pressure.

## Pruned vs. Semi-Pruned, Minimal vs. Non-Minimal SSA

- **Non-minimal SSA**: phi-functions placed at every join point reachable per variable without liveness filtering — more phis than necessary.
- **Semi-pruned SSA**: a cheap pre-pass (traversal of the CFG) removes variables local to a single block (never live across block boundaries) from phi-insertion consideration before running IDF, reducing phi count without full liveness analysis.
- **Pruned SSA**: full liveness analysis is used so phi-functions are inserted only where the variable is actually live, eliminating all dead phis; this is strictly minimal in the sense of liveness but costs a liveness pass.
- **Minimal SSA** (formal sense, per Cytron et al.): the IDF-based placement guarantees exactly one phi per variable per node in IDF(Defs(v)) — the fewest phis consistent with the dominance frontier structure, irrespective of liveness; it may still contain phis for dead variables, which pruning removes.

Braun et al.'s algorithm, via trivial-phi elimination, achieves minimality incrementally and locally without computing dominance frontiers, converging to the same minimal set of non-redundant phis that the Cytron IDF construction yields directly, up to removal of phis for variables not actually live (which still requires a separate liveness/pruning pass if strict pruned-SSA is desired).

# Register Allocation: Graph-Coloring, Linear Scan, and SSA-Based Approaches

## Chaitin-Briggs Graph-Coloring Allocation

The classical formulation, due to Chaitin et al. (1981) and refined by Briggs et al. (1994), models register allocation as graph coloring. After instruction selection, the compiler computes **live ranges** (webs) for each virtual register via liveness analysis (backward dataflow computing `live-in`/`live-out` sets per basic block). The **interference graph** has one node per live range, with an edge between two ranges that are simultaneously live and cannot share a register — classically, two ranges interfere if one is live at a definition point of the other where they hold different values (precise interference, as opposed to the coarser "live at the same program point" approximation).

The allocator then runs the **simplify-spill-select** worklist loop:

- **Simplify**: repeatedly remove any node of degree < k (k = number of available physical registers) from the graph, pushing it onto a stack. Low-degree nodes are trivially colorable later because fewer than k neighbors can conflict.
- **Spill** (Chaitin's original version): when no low-degree node remains, pick a node by a **spill cost heuristic** — typically `cost = (def_weight + use_weight) / degree`, where def/use weight accounts for execution frequency (loop nesting depth, often weighted 10^depth) — and optimistically mark it for potential spill, removing it to continue simplification. Chaitin's original algorithm commits to spilling immediately; Briggs introduced **optimistic coloring**: high-degree nodes are pushed onto the stack too (not immediately spilled), deferring the spill decision to the select phase.
- **Select**: pop nodes off the stack and assign colors (physical registers) greedily, avoiding colors used by already-colored neighbors. Under optimistic coloring, a node pushed as "potential spill" may still find a free color at select time if its neighbors ended up using fewer than k distinct colors — this is the key improvement Briggs made over Chaitin, reducing unnecessary spills.
- If a node truly has no available color, it is **actually spilled**: a new virtual register is introduced, spill/reload (store/load) code is inserted around each def/use, and the interference graph is rebuilt (or incrementally patched) for another simplify-spill-select pass.

**Coalescing** merges move-related nodes (source and destination of a `copy`/`mov` instruction) into one node when safe, eliminating the move. **Chaitin coalescing** merges aggressively whenever the two nodes don't interfere, but this can increase the merged node's degree and induce additional spills. **Briggs (conservative) coalescing** only merges if the resulting node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k, guaranteeing simplification isn't harmed. **George coalescing** is a related conservative criterion checking each neighbor of one node individually against the other's neighbor set. **Biased coloring** is a cheaper alternative to coalescing: during select, prefer assigning a color already used by a move-related neighbor, achieving many of coalescing's benefits without graph restructuring.

## Linear Scan Allocation

Linear scan (Poletto & Sarkar, 1999) trades optimality for speed, making it standard in JIT compilers (e.g., early HotSpot client compiler, V8's Crankshaft/Turbofan, LuaJIT, and until recently LLVM's fast allocator for `-O0`). It computes **live intervals**: for each virtual register, a single contiguous range `[start, end]` over a linear instruction numbering (not full SSA liveness), approximating true (possibly non-contiguous) liveness as one interval, optionally with "lifetime holes."

Intervals are sorted by start point and scanned left to right, maintaining an **active list** of intervals currently live, kept sorted by end point. At each new interval's start, expired intervals (end point < current start) are removed from active, freeing their registers. If `|active| == k` when a new interval begins, a spill decision is made: the heuristic spills the interval with the **furthest next use point** (or furthest end point in the original algorithm) among active intervals and the new one, since spilling it delays the reload longest and minimizes spill code impact — this is the same intuition as Belady's farthest-in-future page replacement.

**Second-chance (extended) linear scan**, also from Poletto & Sarkar, splits a live interval at the spill point rather than spilling it entirely for its whole lifetime: the portion before the spill point keeps its register, and a new interval (reload) is created for the remainder, potentially getting a register again later ("second chance"). This is an early, restricted form of **live-range splitting**.

## SSA-Based Graph Coloring and LLVM's Greedy Allocator

A key theoretical result (Brisk et al.; Hack, Grund, Goos) is that the interference graph of values in **strict SSA form** is **chordal** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord), because SSA's dominance-based def-use structure induces a tree-like (dominator-tree) interference structure. Chordal graphs are **perfectly colorable in polynomial time** via a **simplicial elimination ordering** — a greedy coloring following a perfect elimination order always finds the chromatic number, with no need for heuristic spill/select iteration to achieve optimal coloring (modulo spilling for insufficient k). This underlies "SSA re-elimination" allocators that color directly on SSA form, deferring spilling and coalescing (out-of-SSA copy insertion / phi elimination) as separate concerns, and gives rise to **puzzle-based** register assignment formulations exploiting the tree-width-bounded structure for architectures with irregular register classes (e.g., aliasing, paired registers).

LLVM's `RAGreedy` allocator is SSA-aware but not chordal-coloring-based directly; instead it uses **interval-based eviction** over `LiveInterval`s computed on SSA-derived virtual registers, processing a priority queue ordered by **spill weight** (a frequency- and size-normalized cost estimate). # Alias Analysis: Precision/Scalability Tradeoffs Across Analysis Families

Alias analysis determines whether two pointer expressions can, must, or cannot refer to the same memory location, feeding downstream optimizations (dead store elimination, load/store forwarding, LICM, vectorization, instruction scheduling) with the memory-dependence facts needed to reorder or eliminate memory operations soundly.

## Andersen's Inclusion-Based Analysis

Andersen's analysis (1994) is **flow-insensitive** and **inclusion-based**: each program variable `p` is assigned an abstract points-to set `pts(p)`, and each pointer assignment is translated into a **subset constraint** over these sets rather than an equality. The four canonical constraint forms are:

- `p = &a` → `a ∈ pts(p)` (base constraint)
- `p = q` → `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)` (copy constraint)
- `p = *q` → for all `a ∈ pts(q)`, `pts(a) ⊆ pts(p)` (load constraint)
- `*p = q` → for all `a ∈ pts(p)`, `pts(q) ⊆ pts(a)` (store constraint)

These constraints are represented as a **constraint graph**: nodes are abstract locations/variables, and copy edges `q → p` encode `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)`. Solving is a **worklist-based fixpoint propagation**: when a node's points-to set grows, its new elements are pushed along outgoing edges to successors, and dereference constraints (load/store) may dynamically add new edges to the graph as points-to sets grow — this dynamic edge addition is what distinguishes Andersen's from a static dataflow problem. The process iterates until no set changes, producing a sound (over-approximate) **may-alias** solution.

**Cycle elimination** is the key scalability optimization: a cycle in the constraint graph (common from loops of assignments like `p = q; q = p;`) implies all nodes on the cycle must have identical points-to sets, so they can be collapsed into one representative node (detected via, e.g., Tarjan's SCC algorithm applied online, as in Pearce/Kelly/Hankin or Hardekopf/Lin's "Lin-Andersen"), shrinking the graph and avoiding redundant propagation. Without such collapsing, the algorithm still terminates but repeats work across cycle members.

Complexity is bounded by **O(n³)** in the number of variables: there are O(n²) possible points-to pairs, and each pair can trigger propagation along O(n) edges in the worst case. Hardekopf and Lin's "bit vectors and sparse bitmaps" and **wave propagation / difference propagation** techniques reduce the practical constant significantly, but the cubic worst case remains the standard citation for whole-program inclusion-based analysis on large C/C++ codebases.

## Steensgaard's Unification-Based Analysis

Steensgaard's analysis (1996) replaces subset constraints with **equality constraints**: whenever two pointers may point to overlapping sets, their abstract storage locations are **unified** into a single **equivalence class** using a **union-find** data structure. A load/store, e.g. `p = *q`, unifies the "points-to target" type of `q` with `p`'s own abstract location, rather than propagating individual facts. Because union-find supports near-constant amortized `find`/`union` operations (with path compression and union-by-rank), the overall algorithm runs in **O(n α(n))**, i.e., near-linear time, with `α` the inverse Ackermann function.

The precision cost is substantial: unification is **not distributive** — once two variables are merged into one equivalence class, every pointer that *either* may point to becomes a pointer that *both* are considered to point to, permanently conflating their points-to sets for the rest of the analysis. This is the core precision loss relative to Andersen's inclusion-based (subset) formulation, which keeps directionality and therefore can represent "p's targets are a subset of q's targets" without forcing equality. In practice Steensgaard's analysis produces one points-to graph node per "memory cell type" program-wide, giving a much coarser but highly scalable approximation, historically used in tools needing whole-program analysis at compile-time cost closer to linear passes (e.g., early versions of Microsoft's static analysis tooling, `cqual`-style systems).

## Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA)

TBAA assumes (and in C/C++ is licensed by) the **strict aliasing rule**: an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of its **effective type**, a compatible type, a signed/unsigned variant, or `char`/`unsigned char` (the designated universal-access exception). Under this rule, two memory accesses through pointers of unrelated types are statically **no-alias**, independent of any pointer value analysis — this is a purely type-syntactic criterion, not a points-to computation.

LLVM encodes TBAA as **metadata attached to load/store instructions**, structured as a tree: each node names a type and a parent node representing the type it is "contained in" or derived from (its access path toward the root, typically `"any pointer"` or a char-compatible root). Two accesses are TBAA-no-alias if neither metadata node is an ancestor of the other in this tree (i.e., the types are not compatible along the subtyping/containment path). **Struct-path TBAA** (sometimes called "path-sensitive" or field-aware TBAA, introduced to fix unsoundness in the original flat TBAA) refines this by encoding the full **access path** — the sequence of struct fields traversed to reach the accessed memory, including base type, offset, and field type — so that accesses to `a.x` and `a.y` within the same struct `a` are correctly distinguished as no-alias even though both ultimately derive from the same aggregate type. Each struct-path node records `(base-type, field-offset, field-type)`, and alias queries compare offset-qualified paths rather than bare types.

## Cross-Cutting Dimensions and Consumers

Orthogonal to the specific algorithm, analyses vary along:

- **Flow-sensitivity**: flow-sensitive analysis computes a distinct points-to state per program point (tracking strong updates after a definite pointer assignment), while flow-insensitive analysis (both classical Andersen's and Steensgaard's) computes one set per variable valid for the whole program, only ever performing **weak updates** (union, never kill).
- **Context-sensitivity**: distinguishes calling contexts rather than merging all call sites into one summary. **k-CFA** parameterizes context by the last k call sites (or allocation sites) encountered; the simpler **call-string approach** tracks a bounded-length string of call-site labels as context identifier, cloning analysis facts per distinct string to avoid merging unrelated callers at a shared callee.
- **Field-sensitivity**: distinguishes individual struct/array fields as separate abstract locations (as struct-path TBAA does) versus collapsing an aggregate to one location (field-insensitive), trading precision for state-space size.
- **Alias query results**: classified as **must-alias** (always the same location), **may-alias** (possibly the same, cannot be ruled out), or **no-alias** (provably distinct). Must-alias licenses strong updates and store-to-load forwarding; no-alias licenses reordering and independence; may-alias forces conservative dependence edges.

These results populate **alias sets** (LLVM's `AliasSetTracker`-style grouping of memory operations known to mutually may-alias) used by memory dependence analysis for instruction scheduling and vectorization — a scheduler or vectorizer may only reorder or pack memory operations across an alias-set boundary when no-alias is established. Concretely: **load/store forwarding** requires must-alias between a store and a subsequent load to substitute the stored value directly; **dead store elimination** requires proving a store is must-alias (or at least not-may-alias-escaped) with respect to all subsequent reads before the next overwrite, so it can be removed as unobserved; and **LICM** requires proving a memory location accessed inside a loop is not may-aliased by any other store within the loop body (or is invariant) before hoisting the load above the loop or sinking a redundant store below it.

# Register Allocation: Graph-Coloring, Linear Scan, and SSA-Based Approaches

## Chaitin-Briggs Graph-Coloring Allocation

The classical formulation, due to Chaitin et al. (1981) and refined by Briggs et al. (1994), models register allocation as graph coloring. After instruction selection, the compiler computes **live ranges** (webs) for each virtual register via liveness analysis (backward dataflow computing `live-in`/`live-out` sets per basic block). The **interference graph** has one node per live range, with an edge between two ranges that are simultaneously live and cannot share a register — classically, two ranges interfere if one is live at a definition point of the other where they hold different values (precise interference, as opposed to the coarser "live at the same program point" approximation).

The allocator then runs the **simplify-spill-select** worklist loop:

- **Simplify**: repeatedly remove any node of degree < k (k = number of available physical registers) from the graph, pushing it onto a stack. Low-degree nodes are trivially colorable later because fewer than k neighbors can conflict.
- **Spill** (Chaitin's original version): when no low-degree node remains, pick a node by a **spill cost heuristic** — typically `cost = (def_weight + use_weight) / degree`, where def/use weight accounts for execution frequency (loop nesting depth, often weighted 10^depth) — and optimistically mark it for potential spill, removing it to continue simplification. Chaitin's original algorithm commits to spilling immediately; Briggs introduced **optimistic coloring**: high-degree nodes are pushed onto the stack too (not immediately spilled), deferring the spill decision to the select phase.
- **Select**: pop nodes off the stack and assign colors (physical registers) greedily, avoiding colors used by already-colored neighbors. Under optimistic coloring, a node pushed as "potential spill" may still find a free color at select time if its neighbors ended up using fewer than k distinct colors — this is the key improvement Briggs made over Chaitin, reducing unnecessary spills.
- If a node truly has no available color, it is **actually spilled**: a new virtual register is introduced, spill/reload (store/load) code is inserted around each def/use, and the interference graph is rebuilt (or incrementally patched) for another simplify-spill-select pass.

**Coalescing** merges move-related nodes (source and destination of a `copy`/`mov` instruction) into one node when safe, eliminating the move. **Chaitin coalescing** merges aggressively whenever the two nodes don't interfere, but this can increase the merged node's degree and induce additional spills. **Briggs (conservative) coalescing** only merges if the resulting node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k, guaranteeing simplification isn't harmed. **George coalescing** is a related conservative criterion checking each neighbor of one node individually against the other's neighbor set. **Biased coloring** is a cheaper alternative to coalescing: during select, prefer assigning a color already used by a move-related neighbor, achieving many of coalescing's benefits without graph restructuring.

Linear scan (Poletto & Sarkar, 1999) trades optimality for speed, making it standard in JIT compilers (e.g., early HotSpot client compiler, V8's Crankshaft/Turbofan, LuaJIT, and until recently LLVM's fast allocator for `-O0`). Intervals are sorted by start point and scanned left to right, maintaining an **active list** of intervals currently live, kept sorted by end point. At each new interval's start, expired intervals (end point < current start) are removed from active, freeing their registers. If `|active| == k` when a new interval begins, a spill decision is made: the heuristic spills the interval with the **furthest next use point** (or furthest end point in the original algorithm) among active intervals and the new one, since spilling it delays the reload longest and minimizes spill code impact — this is the same intuition as Belady's farthest-in-future page replacement.

**Second-chance (extended) linear scan**, also from Poletto & Sarkar, splits a live interval at the spill point rather than spilling it entirely for its whole lifetime: the portion before the spill point keeps its register, and a new interval (reload) is created for the remainder, potentially getting a register again later ("second chance"). This is an early, restricted form of **live-range splitting**.

When no physical register is free, it attempts to **evict** a lower-weight already-assigned interval, or falls back to **live-range splitting** — region splitting, local splitting, and basic-block splitting — to shrink an interval's footprint until it fits available register classes, deferring actual spill-code insertion as a last resort and using **rematerialization** (recomputing a value from cheap inputs, e.g., a constant load, instead of spilling/reloading) whenever the defining instruction is cheap and side-effect-free.
